doc.title: Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Oneonta, New York, December 28, 2005

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: When you — I’m going to leap ahead a little bit — but you’ve seen an awful lot of changes in this country: technology and social issues and all that. Are there certain things that stand out in your head as being really memorable and unbelievable changes over the years?

Oh my God. Unbelievable is like I remember one instance, when tape recorders came out. There were wire. An actual wire. And the music was on the wire. But it sounded raspy. It was raspy. And shortly after that came the ribbon. And they got better and better and better. And now you can buy little boxes that have a wonderful sound. Yes. I know we didn’t even have a phonograph. Yeah, I’m sorry I take that — we had the wind-up phonograph.
But when I think of the 78s which we have some, and you had one song on each side.
And they were heavy to carry around.
